records.record_text: The object of the mercenary aggression was to overthrow the Government of Seychelles and, it seems, install Mr. James Mancham as head of State.
The leader of the mercenaries was Michael Hoare, who had led earlier mercenary operations in Africa.
The immediate preparations for and planning of the mercenary aggression, including recruitment of over 50 mercenaries by Hoare, took place in South Africa.
records.policy_implication: Implicates South Africa as the staging ground for the aggression.

records.record_text: Given the tight and effective control exercised by the security authorities in South Africa, and the nature of the preparations for the mercenary operation... the Commission finds it difficult to believe that the South African authorities did not at least have knowledge of the preparations in this matter.
records.political_signal: The Commission casts serious doubt on the South African government's denial of knowledge, implying potential complicity.
records.policy_implication: Raises questions about state responsibility and the need for accountability for states that harbor or fail to prevent mercenary activities.

records.record_text: On the basis of information available to it at the time of submission of this report, the Commission cannot reach a definitive conclusion on the extent or level of South African knowledge or responsibility.
records.political_signal: Highlights the limitations of the investigation and the incomplete nature of the findings regarding a key aspect of the mandate.
records.policy_implication: Indicates that a crucial part of the truth remains unconfirmed due to lack of full cooperation from a Member State.

records.record_text: The Commission was unfortunately limited in its investigations by not being permitted to interview the mercenaries who returned to South Africa aboard the hijacked Air India plane. In particular it was handicapped by not having an interview with the leader of the mercenaries, Michael Hoare.
records.political_signal: Directly calls out the lack of cooperation from South Africa, which impeded the fulfillment of the Commission's mandate.
records.policy_implication: The inability to access key witnesses fundamentally weakened the Commission's ability to provide a complete and definitive report on the origin and financing of the attack.

records.record_text: The aggression posed a grave threat to the sovereignty and independence of the country and seriously disrupted its daily life. This event underscores the vulnerability of small States, particularly those in geographical situations such as that of Seychelles, to aggression by mercenaries.
records.policy_implication: Highlights a systemic weakness in the international system regarding the protection of small states from non-state and state-sponsored aggression.

records.record_text: As regards the financing, the Commission estimates, on the basis of information available to it, that the expenses incurred in the mercenary operation... would have amounted to at least three quarters of a million dollars.
The Commission did not receive information to enable it to identify such sources [of finance].
records.policy_implication: Another key aspect of the mandate—identifying the financing—remains unfulfilled.

records.record_text: The Commission believes that the mercenaries used Swaziland merely as a means of transit to Seychelles and that the Government of Swaziland had no knowledge of the planned aggression until after it had taken place.
records.political_signal: Exonerates the Government of Swaziland from any complicity in the attack.

records.record_text: As regards statements made to the Commission that had the mercenary aggression been successful contingents of armed personnel might have been flown from Kenya, the Commission would draw attention to the exchange of communications between the Commission and the Government of Kenya and to the statement made by the Government of Kenya on 8 December 1981 categorically denying any involvement...
records.political_signal: The Commission reports the allegation and the denial without making its own assessment, thereby leaving the question open but formally acknowledging Kenya's position.

records.record_text: On the assumption that the number of tourist arrivals would decline by approximately 18 per cent, the Seychelles Government anticipates a total loss to the economy of R101 million or about $16.7 million, taking into account the loss of tourism revenue and its multiplier effect on the economy.
records.policy_implication: Quantifies the severe economic impact of the attack, forming the basis for the recommendation for financial assistance.

records.record_text: It is clear that there will be a significant adverse impact on the Seychelles economy resulting from the aggression.

The Commission recommends that financial, technical and material assistance should be provided urgently by Member States and international organisations to enable the country to deal with the difficulties it is facing because of the mercenary aggression.

The Commission recommends that the work at present under way on an international convention against the recruitment, use, financing and training of mercenaries be brought to a speedy conclusion so that the convention may be opened for signature as soon as possible.
records.political_signal: Signals the inadequacy of the existing legal framework and the urgent need for a dedicated international instrument to combat mercenarism.
records.policy_implication: Calls for prioritizing the finalization of the Anti-Mercenary Convention within the UN system.

records.record_text: The Commission also wishes to recommend that States, and the international community as a whole, should make every effort to prevent mercenary operations, having regard to the grave threat which these operations pose particularly to small island States with limited resources, such as the Republic of Seychelles.

It is also the view of the Commission that ICAO should, in the light of the apparent ease with which weapons can be transported in checked baggage on commercial airlines, give further consideration to preventive measures, while taking into account the wish of Governments to facilitate tourism.
records.policy_implication: Identifies a major security loophole in international civil aviation and calls for a review of global standards.

records.record_text: Should the Security Council so desire, the Commission might be authorized to furnish a supplementary report in due course containing any further information relative to its mandate.
records.political_signal: Signals that the Commission believes more information may emerge (e.g., from the South African trial) and that its work is not definitively complete.

records.record_text: Martin Dolinschek, who is in custody in Seychelles, stated to the Commission that he was a serving member of the National Intelligence Service of South Africa. He further stated that he had informed his superiors about previous plots by Seychellois exiles to overthrow the Government of Seychelles, but that he had not done so on this occasion, although he believed they knew about the plans otherwise.
records.political_signal: Direct testimony alleging South African intelligence awareness and involvement.

records.record_text: The Director of the National Intelligence Service [of South Africa] refused, as a matter of policy, to confirm or deny that Dolinschek was an official of the Service.
records.actor_source: Head of National Intelligence Service of South Africa (Dr. Lucas D. Barnard)
records.political_signal: South Africa's refusal to clarify the status of an alleged intelligence agent involved in the attack is a form of non-cooperation.

mission_title: Report of the Security Council mission established pursuant to resolution 819 (1993)
mission_country_or_region: Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro)

mission_analytics.mission_subtype: Situation Assessment, Political Engagement, Investigative
main_risks: Catastrophic humanitarian conditions in Srebrenica (lack of water, sanitation, medical care) leading to potential epidemics and a 'slow-motion process of genocide'.
Bosnian Serb forces increasing pressure on Srebrenica in defiance of UNSC resolution 819 and showing little respect for UN authority.
The spread of conflict and atrocities to other vulnerable enclaves like Gorazde, Zepa, and Tuzla.
UNPROFOR's mandate being too restrictive to protect civilians or enforce 'safe areas', leading to frustration among troops and an inability to counter defiance.
The outbreak of conflict between Bosnian Croat and Bosnian government forces, involving atrocities and threatening the Vance-Owen plan.
main_commitments: The Bosnian Serb leader, Dr. Karadžić, indicated that the water supply to Srebrenica would be restored and humanitarian convoys allowed, subject to inspection.
President Izetbegović and Mr. Mate Boban agreed to create a joint command for their armies and cease hostilities between them, and to move forward with implementing the Vance-Owen plan.
President Tudjman of Croatia promised to use his influence to see that those guilty of atrocities against Muslims were punished.
main_policy_signals: The mission's visit itself was a strong political signal of the Security Council's engagement and a 'symbol of hope' for the Bosnian population.
Direct condemnation was delivered to Bosnian Croat leaders for atrocities, warning of repercussions.
The Srebrenica 'safe area' arrangement was not considered a model for the future.

The Council was considering a graduated response to non-compliance, with the establishment of more robust safe areas as a step short of immediate military strikes, but with the intent to enforce them if necessary.
The Council should be kept more fully informed by the field to effectively discharge its responsibilities.
mission_analytics.summary_assessment: The Security Council mission conducted an extensive field visit to assess the dire humanitarian situation in Srebrenica and other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and to investigate reports of atrocities. The mission found Srebrenica to be an 'open jail' where Bosnian Serb forces were increasing pressure in defiance of Resolution 819, creating a 'slow-motion process of genocide'. The mission also confirmed atrocities committed by Bosnian Croat forces against Muslims in central Bosnia. The report's central recommendations are to urgently declare Sarajevo, Gorazde, Zepa, and Tuzla as 'safe areas' and to revise UNPROFOR's mandate to give it the capability and authority to enforce these zones, including through credible deterrence. The mission served as a powerful political signal of Council concern and explored a graduated response strategy, positioning 'safe areas' as a preventive measure that stopped short of immediate large-scale military intervention but required a clear intent to enforce.

activities.activity_description: Briefing at UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb by the Force Commander and senior staff.
Meeting with President Izetbegović of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo.
Briefing in Kiseljak by the Chief of Staff of BH Command, the UNHCR Coordinator, and the ICRC Coordinator.
Briefing in Vitez by the Commanding Officer of the British Battalion.
Visit to Ahinici to a house where an entire family had been killed.
Meeting in Srebrenica with senior representatives of the Bosnian Serb Army and the Bosnian Army.
Briefing in Srebrenica by the Commanding Officer of the Canadian Battalion, UNHCR, and ICRC.
Visit to an UNPROFOR observation post in the mountains surrounding Srebrenica.
Brief meeting with the Mayor of Tuzla.
Meeting in Split with Mr. Mate Boban and his military commander.
Meeting at Belgrade airport with Dr. Radovan Karadžić and his Assistant.
Meeting at Zagreb airport with President Tudjman of the Republic of Croatia and his senior advisors.
Meeting at the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb with Vice-President Ganić and a Member of the Presidency.

records.record_text: The killing of civilians by Muslims was viewed by the Serbs as justifying their offensive.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Highlights the cycle of justifications for violence and atrocities.

records.record_text: The assessment of Lieutenant-General Lars-Eric Wahlgren (UNPROFOR Force Commander) is that it all reflected a chain reaction by all parties. In his view, all sides are committing atrocities at different levels, but only Serbs are taking territory.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Distinguishes between atrocities committed by all sides and the strategic acquisition of territory primarily by one side, shaping the mission's understanding of the conflict's nature.

records.record_text: The prevailing conditions of overcrowding, lack of drinking water, which has been cut off, the absence of electricity, sanitation and basic medical assistance represent an extraordinarily dramatic and cruel situation for the people of Srebrenica, many of whom are sleeping in the streets.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Establishes the severity of the humanitarian crisis, forming the basis for urgent recommendations.

records.record_text: The damage and destruction of more than 50 per cent of the town’s houses and public facilities are also creating significant health problems and dangerous sanitary conditions, with the possibility that such a hazardous situation might lead to epidemics, as reported by UNHCR and ICRC.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Identifies an imminent public health catastrophe, adding urgency to calls for intervention.

records.record_text: the Serbs are determined to show that they are in effective control of the town, that it is at their mercy and that they have not taken Srebrenica only because of the adoption of Security Council resolution 819 (1993).
records.political_signal: Reports that Serb forces are signaling their dominance and that UNSC action had a deterrent effect.
records.policy_implication: Shows that while the resolution had an impact, Serb forces are defying its spirit and intent, requiring further Council action.

records.record_text: Generals Wahlgren and Morillon stated to the Mission that without such Security Council action the agreement of 18 April 1993 (annex II) between the Bosnian Serbs and the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the demilitarization of Srebrenica would not have been reached.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Provides evidence of the positive impact of Security Council resolutions on achieving ground-level agreements.

records.record_text: upon its return from Srebrenica, the Mission was held in Zvornik against its will for half an hour.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Illustrates the challenging operating environment and the lack of respect for the United Nations by Bosnian Serb forces.

records.record_text: The Council should note that when it was discussing resolution 819 (1993), it did not know that negotiations involving the Force Commander of UNPROFOR had been taking place and that UNPROFOR had participated actively in the drafting and in the process of convincing the Bosnian Commander to sign the agreement.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Points to a communication gap between the field mission and the Security Council, affecting the Council's decision-making process.

records.record_text: Both the President and the Vice-President of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina informed us that they had been reminded by the UNPROFOR officers that no outside support would be forthcoming and that they were evidently defenceless. They had to sign the agreement under duress.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Questions the legitimacy and sustainability of an agreement signed under duress, and highlights the difficult ethical choices faced by UN personnel in the field.

records.record_text: the Mission feels that lessons should be drawn from this experience, both in terms of the need for adequate and opportune information and of the hard choices that may have to be considered.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Calls for improved communication protocols between the field and HQ and for the Council to prepare for difficult policy decisions.

records.record_text: The Srebrenica arrangement cannot be a model but should inspire action by the Security Council to prevent the fall of further enclaves and territories, such as Gorazde, Zepa and Tuzla, which demand immediate action.
records.political_signal: Signals that while the Srebrenica outcome was suboptimal, the concept of protected areas should be applied elsewhere proactively.
records.policy_implication: Proposes a shift from reactive to preventive action by the Security Council regarding vulnerable enclaves.

records.record_text: Srebrenica is today the equivalent of an open jail in which its people can wander around but are controlled and terrorized by the increasing presence of Serb tanks and other heavy weapons in its immediate surroundings. The UNHCR representative described the town as a 'bad refugee camp'.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Conveys the failure of the 'safe area' in its current form to provide genuine security or freedom for the population, undermining the intent of Resolution 819.

records.record_text: To impede medical assistance is a crime of genocide. This action, together with the cutting of the water supply and electricity, have put into effect a slow-motion process of genocide.
records.political_signal: Uses highly charged legal terminology to signal the extreme gravity of the situation.
records.policy_implication: Raises the legal and moral stakes for the Security Council, implying that failure to act could be seen as complicity in genocide.

records.record_text: Evidently the Serb paramilitary forces not only are not withdrawing as demanded by resolution 819 (1993) but are increasing their pressure on the town.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Documents a clear violation of a key demand in Resolution 819, requiring a response from the Council.

records.record_text: The attitude of defiance of the Serbs towards the United Nations in general is a matter that should concern the Council. The Serbs obviously have little respect for UNPROFOR’s authority.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Highlights a fundamental challenge to the UN's credibility and effectiveness, suggesting that the current approach is failing to command respect or compliance.

records.record_text: The Mission believes, as does UNPROFOR, that the actual 4 1/2 by 1/2 kilometres decided as a safe area should be greatly expanded.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Calls for a specific, practical change to the 'safe area' parameters to make it more viable.

records.record_text: The water supply must be resumed. Today this is - if possible - of greater human value and priority than the withdrawal of the Serb forces. Cutting off the water supply is a criminal practice and the Council should demand its immediate cessation.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Identifies the most critical immediate humanitarian need and frames it as a 'criminal practice' requiring an explicit Council demand.

records.record_text: The Mission feels that the Security Council should also be kept more fully informed of developments and consulted accordingly - not with a view to 'micro-managing' but in order to be in a position to discharge its responsibilities effectively.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Advocates for a systemic change in communication and consultation between the field and the Council.

records.record_text: A Security Council resolution to declare them [Gorazde and Zepa] safe areas should be considered without delay in consultation with UNPROFOR.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Proposes extending the 'safe area' concept as a preventive measure.

records.record_text: The Mission also recommends that it [Tuzla] be declared a safe area.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Proposes extending the 'safe area' concept to a major city hosting a large number of displaced persons.

records.record_text: This capital of all the peoples of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina [Sarajevo] should immediately become a safe area.
records.political_signal: Positions the protection of Sarajevo as a symbolic act to preserve the country's multi-ethnic character.
records.policy_implication: Elevates the status of Sarajevo, urging its protection not just for humanitarian reasons but for its political and symbolic importance.

records.record_text: Mr. Boban, while expressing his condemnation of these acts, nevertheless stated that 'one must not look only to the effects but to the causes', and that 'Croats have been massacred by Muslims'.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Demonstrates the leader's attempt to deflect responsibility and contextualize atrocities, indicating a low likelihood of accountability without external pressure.

records.record_text: President Tudjman also expressed his fears of the expansion of Serbia, which threatened the area of Krajina in Croatia. He said that the Serbs were convinced that the world community would not employ force. It was therefore necessary that pressure be brought to bear upon them. This could be achieved by air strikes on their supplies to Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: A key regional actor is advocating for military enforcement action against the Serbs, adding to the international debate on intervention.

records.record_text: is the restriction of its [UNPROFOR's] role essentially to a supportive humanitarian one, viable in the deteriorating circumstances in Bosnia? Several soldiers in the field expressed deep frustration and anguish to members of the Mission with regard to the restrictions under which they operate.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Questions the fundamental viability of the UNPROFOR mandate and highlights a crisis of morale and purpose within the force.

records.record_text: The Mission believes that the imminent renewal by the Security Council of UNPROFOR’s mandate should be the occasion for the Council to address the following issues in detail: ... a revised mandate, based on speedy recommendation from the Secretary-General and UNPROFOR’s Force Commander, would be urgently required
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Formally proposes that the upcoming mandate renewal be used as the vehicle for a fundamental reassessment and strengthening of UNPROFOR's role.

records.record_text: In the Mission’s view, serious attention needs to be given to bestowing a greater reconnaissance capability upon UNPROFOR - even in a situation where no change in its role was envisaged
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Recommends a specific technical enhancement for the mission to improve its monitoring and information-gathering capacity, regardless of broader mandate changes.

records.record_text: in any resolution to give effect to such designation [of safe areas], it should be clearly and emphatically recorded that the establishment of Security Council safe areas in no way undermines the proposed settlement details of the Vance-Owen plan.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Provides specific drafting language to ensure that interim security measures are not misconstrued as prejudging the final political settlement.

records.record_text: It [a decision to create robust safe areas] would not rule out eventual consideration of such measures [military strikes] - but at a next stage, if the Serbs simply ignored the integrity of Security Council safe areas; nor would it, on the other hand, automatically predetermine a move to military strikes.
records.actor_target: Security Council, Parties to the conflict
records.political_signal: Outlines a strategy of graduated response, positioning 'safe areas' as an intermediate step and implicitly warning of potential escalation to military strikes in case of non-compliance.
records.policy_implication: The mission is offering the Council a policy pathway that increases pressure and enforcement without immediately resorting to the most forceful options.

records.record_text: Designation of Security Council safe areas would have to be done with the clear intent that they would, once established, be enforced or defended if need be.
records.political_signal: null
records.policy_implication: Argues that for the 'safe area' concept to be effective, it must be backed by credible military deterrence, a significant shift from a purely humanitarian or monitoring role.

mission_title: Report of the Security Council Ad Hoc Committee established under resolution 455 (1979), concerning the complaint by Zambia, to assist the Security Council in the implementation of the resolution

mission_analytics.mission_subtype: Fact-finding and Resource Mobilization
main_risks: Continued aggression by Southern Rhodesia and South Africa aimed at destroying Zambia's economic infrastructure.
Broader regional destabilization due to South Africa's policy of creating 'puppet States' and interfering in neighboring countries.
Severe economic crisis in Zambia due to the disruption of vital transport links, potentially leading to shortages of food and essential goods.
main_commitments: The Ad Hoc Committee committed to fulfilling its mandate by assessing damage and mobilizing international assistance for Zambia.
Several Member States and the European Economic Community committed significant financial and material aid for the reconstruction of Zambia's bridges.
The Government of Zambia expressed its determination to rebuild the destroyed infrastructure as a national priority, regardless of future attacks.
main_policy_signals: The Security Council's establishment of the Ad Hoc Committee signaled strong international support for Zambia and condemnation of the aggression by Southern Rhodesia.
Zambia signaled its continued commitment to UN principles, including sanctions against Southern Rhodesia, despite suffering severe consequences.
President Kaunda identified South Africa as the primary threat to regional peace and security, accusing it of a strategy to create dependent puppet states.
mission_analytics.summary_assessment: The Ad Hoc Committee, established by SCR 455 (1979), conducted a mission to Zambia to assess the damage from acts of aggression by Southern Rhodesia and to mobilize international assistance. The mission combined fact-finding, including site visits to destroyed bridges, with high-level engagement with the Zambian government and outreach to donors. The report documents the severe economic impact of the destruction of Zambia's transport infrastructure, framing the issue as a threat to regional peace and security. The Committee successfully facilitated the mobilization of significant international aid for bridge reconstruction, fulfilling a key part of its mandate.

activities.activity_description: Held three meetings in New York to examine terms of reference, determine procedure, and establish a schedule of activities (3-6 December 1979).
The Ad Hoc Committee visited Zambia from 11 to 14 December 1979.
Received a briefing from the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Zambia on the situation resulting from the blowing up of the bridges (11 December 1979).
Held meetings with the President of the Republic of Zambia, Dr. Kenneth D. Kaunda (13 December 1979).
Held meetings with senior Government officials, including Ministers and Permanent Secretaries from various ministries (11 and 14 December 1979).
Met with representatives of United Nations agencies based in Zambia (13 December 1979).
Met on an informal basis with representatives of some countries which either had already pledged assistance to Zambia or could be considered potential donors (13 December 1979).
Visited the sites of damaged rail and road bridges over the Chambeshi and Lunsemfwa rivers, the Kaleya road bridge, and the Chongwe road bridge (12, 13, and 14 December 1979).
Held its 5th meeting in Lusaka and adopted its second interim report (14 December 1979).
Held a press conference in Lusaka before departing (14 December 1979).
The Chairman conducted contacts with Member States and international organizations after the visit to secure assistance for Zambia via letters and approaches to Permanent Representatives.
Held its 6th meeting in New York and adopted its final report (31 January 1980).

Senior Zambian Government Officials (Secretary to the Cabinet, Permanent Secretaries, etc.)
Representatives of United Nations agencies (ECA, FAO, IBRD, ILO, UNCN, UNDP, UNFPA, UNHCR, UNICEF, UNIDO, WFP, WHO)
Representatives of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

records.record_text: In the course of its work, especially during its visit to Zambia, the Ad Hoc Committee obtained information showing that Zambia had suffered severe economic losses as a result of repeated acts of aggression by the illegal regime in Southern Rhodesia.

President Kaunda stressed that South Africa constituted the principal danger to the region; it intended to create puppet régimes in the southern part of Africa and gave support to and trained reactionary forces trying to upset the Governments in Angola, Zambia and Mozambique. ... South Africa's goal of the creation of a constellation of puppet States around it was, he said, the gravest danger to peace and security in southern Africa.
records.political_signal: Identifies South Africa as the primary regional destabilizer, escalating the issue beyond the Southern Rhodesia conflict.
records.policy_implication: Suggests that resolving the Southern Rhodesia issue alone will not bring peace to the region.

records.record_text: The effects on the Zambian industries were very serious. Because huge tonnages of imports were tied up at the various ports, Zambia's industries were unable to produce to capacity and consequently, either had to lay off a large number of workers or ... incur considerable and unjustifiable expense as a result of keeping idle labour. Furthermore, Zambia was facing inevitable shortages of essential commodities, since none of the industries was producing at full capacity. Especially harsh was the shortage of maize, a staple food for Zambia.
records.policy_implication: The attacks created a cascading economic and humanitarian crisis affecting industry, employment, and food security.

records.record_text: To repair the direct physical damage, without any expansion or other improvement of the 11 bridges, Zambia needed, at current costs, 14,618,000 kwachas, including consultancy expenses and allocations for contingencies.
records.policy_implication: Provides a specific financial target for international assistance for the most urgent reconstruction needs.

records.record_text: The Ad Hoc Committee saw the degree of destruction brought about by the Rhodesian raids and the hardships caused to the people of Zambia. It also witnessed the determination with which the people of Zambia were pursuing the task of rebuilding the bridges, even with insufficient resources.
records.policy_implication: Direct observation by the Committee corroborates the severity of the damage and validates Zambia's need for assistance.

records.record_text: The Government of Zambia and the Zambian people have undertaken urgent measures towards overcoming the losses and material hardships suffered by Zambia, putting the emphasis on the immediate need to restore the damaged bridges, but the prevailing economic situation does not enable the Zambian people to carry this burden by themselves.
records.policy_implication: Justifies the need for international assistance by assessing that Zambia's national capacity is insufficient for the recovery task.

records.record_text: The Ad Hoc Committee, nevertheless, would like to stress the continued need for further assistance from Member States and international organizations to Zambia in order to facilitate the reconstruction of the economic infrastructure of Zambia.
records.policy_implication: Indicates that while initial fundraising was successful, the reconstruction needs are ongoing and require sustained support.

records.record_text: The Government of Zambia regarded the speedy restoration of the damaged bridges as an absolute necessity for the survival of the national economy. Even if the Rhodesian rebels returned and destroyed the reconstructed bridges again, Zambia would have no choice but to start rebuilding them once again. The Government and the people of Zambia were determined to meet that task as their highest priority.
records.political_signal: Demonstrates Zambia's resilience and unwavering commitment to its economic independence in the face of aggression.

records.record_text: In the view of the Ad Hoc Committee, the response of Member States and international organizations to the appeal by the Security Council for material and other forms of assistance to Zambia (see para. 50 below) has been most encouraging, in particular when related to the target of 14,610,000 kwachas laid down by the Zambian authorities for assistance to restore the damaged bridges. That target has been achieved.
records.political_signal: Highlights the success of the Security Council's resolution and the Committee's work in mobilizing international support.

records.record_text: President Kaunda affirmed once again Zambia's faith in the United Nations... Zambia had carried out sanctions against Southern Rhodesia loyally and faithfully not for reasons of expediency but out of its commitment to the principles of the United Nations Charter. The recent destruction of numerous rail and road bridges was part of the punishment Zambia had suffered for its loyalty to the United Nations.
records.political_signal: Positions Zambia as a loyal UN member being punished for upholding UN sanctions, thereby strengthening its moral and political case for international assistance.

records.record_text: After consideration of the mandate contained in paragraph 5 of resolution 455 (1979), the Ad Hoc Committee, through its Chairman, approached the representatives of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and Zambia, who reaffirmed their positions, as stated at the 2171st meeting of the Security Council on 23 November 1979.
records.policy_implication: Indicates a lack of progress or resolution on the issue of compensation from 'the responsible authorities' (implicating the UK as the administering power), with both parties maintaining their original stances.

records.record_text: The [Zambian] officials emphasized in that connexion that donors should be requested to make their allocations from special funds rather than from funds already allocated to Zambia, for the country could not divert any funds from regular aid for purposes of the current crisis.
records.policy_implication: This is a request for 'additionality' in aid, ensuring that emergency assistance does not compromise long-term development programs.

mission_title: REPORT OF THE SECURITY COUNCIL COMMISSION ESTABLISHED UNDER RESOLUTION 446 (1979)

mission_analytics.mission_subtype: Fact-finding
main_risks: The settlement policy is a 'serious obstruction' to peace and creates 'despair and helplessness' among Palestinians.
The policy is causing 'profound and irreversible' demographic and geographic changes in the occupied territories.
The use of coercive methods, including control of water resources and property seizure, violates basic human rights and international law.
main_commitments: The Commission recommended that the Security Council call on Israel to immediately cease all settlement activities.
The Commission recommended that the Security Council consider measures to protect seized property and address the status of Jerusalem.
The Commission recommended that the Security Council keep the situation under 'constant survey'.
main_policy_signals: The Commission strongly reaffirmed that Israeli settlements are illegal under the Fourth Geneva Convention and a major obstacle to peace.
Israel's refusal to cooperate with the Commission was highlighted as a significant act of defiance against the Security Council.
The Commission's extensive engagement with the PLO, including its Chairman Yasser Arafat, constituted a significant political signal of the organization's relevance to the conflict.
mission_analytics.summary_assessment: This was an investigative mission established by SCR 446 (1979) to examine Israeli settlements in the occupied Arab territories. Despite being denied access to the territories by Israel, the Commission gathered extensive testimony and evidence in neighbouring states (Jordan, Syria, Lebanon, Egypt) from government officials, PLO representatives, and affected individuals. The report concludes that Israel is engaged in a 'wilful, systematic and large-scale process' of establishing settlements, which it deems illegal under the Fourth Geneva Convention and a 'serious obstruction to peace'. It documents the policy's adverse consequences on the Arab population, including displacement and resource deprivation, and recommends that the Security Council call on Israel to cease all settlement activity immediately and keep the matter under constant review.

activities.activity_description: First meeting of the Commission held in New York on 10 April 1979 to organize its programme of work.
The Commission established direct contacts with the parties involved in the matter with a view to seeking their co-operation.
The Commission entered into consultations with relevant United Nations bodies.
Meeting on 30 April 1979 with members of the office of the Crown Prince of Jordan and with the Jordanian Permanent Representative.
Meeting on 30 April 1979 with the Chairman of the Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People.
Visit to the area from 20 May to 1 June 1979, including the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, the Syrian Arab Republic, Lebanon, and the Arab Republic of Egypt.
Working meeting on 21 May 1979 at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Amman, Jordan with the Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and other officials.
Visit on 21 May 1979 to His Excellency the Prime Minister of Jordan, Mr. Mudar Badran.
Audience on 22 May 1979 with His Majesty King Hussein of Jordan.
Meeting on 24 May 1979 with His Highness Crown Prince Hassan of Jordan.
Visit on 23 May 1979 to the Jordan River Valley area, including the King Hussein Bridge and the village of Deir Alla.
Visit on 24 May 1979 to Schneller Refugee Camp in Jordan.
Held five meetings in Jordan devoted to the hearing of 22 witnesses.
Meeting on 27 May 1979 with Mr. Abdul Halim Khaddam, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Syrian Arab Republic.
Open meeting on 27 May 1979 with a Syrian delegation led by Dr. Haitham Keylani.
Visit on 28 May 1979 to the location of the town of Quneitra in the Golan Heights.
Held hearings in Damascus with 13 witnesses, including former inhabitants of the Golan Heights.
Meeting on 29 May 1979 with Mr. Fouad Boutros, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Lebanon.
Meeting on 29 May 1979 with the Prime Minister of Lebanon, Mr. Salim Al Hoss.
Meeting in Beirut on 30 May 1979 with Mr. Yasser Arafat, Chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organization.
Meeting on 30 May 1979 with Dr. Boutros Ghali, Minister of State for Foreign Affairs of the Arab Republic of Egypt.
Meeting on 31 May 1979 with the Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of Egypt, Dr. Mostafa Khalil.
Held a meeting in Cairo on 31 May 1979 to hear seven witnesses.
Private meeting in Cairo with Dr. Hafez Ghanim, Chairman of the International Law Association, and other members.
Held hearings in Damascus with representatives of the Palestine Liberation Organization.

records.record_text: The policy and practices of Israel in establishing settlements in the Palestinian and other Arab Territories occupied since 1967 have no legal validity and constitute a serious obstruction to achieving a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in the Middle East.
records.political_signal: The finding, originating in the resolution and reaffirmed by the Commission, codifies the Council's legal and political stance on the settlements.
records.policy_implication: Forms the legal basis for Security Council and General Assembly action and resolutions concerning Israeli settlements.

records.record_text: The Commission found evidence that the Israeli Government is engaged in a wilful, systematic and large-scale process of establishing settlements in the occupied territories for which it should bear full responsibility.
records.actor_source: Security Council Commission established under resolution 446 (1979)
records.political_signal: The Commission attributes direct responsibility to the Israeli Government, countering any narrative of settlements as private initiatives.
records.policy_implication: This finding strengthens the basis for holding the state of Israel, rather than individual settlers, accountable for the policy.

records.record_text: The Commission considers that the pattern of that settlement policy... is causing profound and irreversible changes of a geographical and demographic nature in those territories, including Jerusalem.
records.actor_source: Security Council Commission established under resolution 446 (1979)
records.political_signal: The use of 'profound and irreversible' signals an urgent crisis that may foreclose future political solutions, particularly a two-state solution.
records.policy_implication: Suggests that time is running out to preserve the character of the territories and the viability of a future Palestinian state.

records.record_text: The Commission has no doubt that those changes are of such a profound nature that they constitute a violation of the fourth Geneva Convention relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War of 12 August 1949 and of the relevant decisions adopted by the United Nations in the matter.
records.actor_source: Security Council Commission established under resolution 446 (1979)
records.political_signal: The Commission makes a definitive legal judgment, reinforcing the international legal consensus on the illegality of the settlements.
records.policy_implication: Provides a basis for calls for accountability under international humanitarian law.

records.record_text: Israel should be called upon to cease on an urgent basis the establishment, construction and planning of settlements in the occupied territories. The question of the existing settlements would then have to be resolved.
records.actor_source: Security Council Commission established under resolution 446 (1979)
records.political_signal: The recommendation for an immediate and complete halt is the core policy prescription of the report.
records.policy_implication: This sets a clear benchmark for future Security Council resolutions and diplomatic efforts on the issue.

records.record_text: The Council might further wish to consider measures to safeguard the impartial protection of property arbitrarily seized.
records.actor_source: Security Council Commission established under resolution 446 (1979)
records.policy_implication: This suggests the potential for establishing a mechanism, such as a property claims commission or registry, to address the widespread issue of land confiscation.

records.record_text: In view of the magnitude of the problem of settlement and its implications for peace in the region, the Security Council should keep the situation under constant survey.
records.actor_source: Security Council Commission established under resolution 446 (1979)
records.policy_implication: Calls for the issue to remain a standing item on the Security Council's agenda, implying the need for regular reporting and meetings.

records.record_text: The Commission is of the view that a correlation exists between the establishment of Israeli settlements and the displacement of the Arab population.
records.actor_source: Security Council Commission established under resolution 446 (1979)
records.political_signal: Directly links settlement construction to the Palestinian refugee problem and internal displacement, challenging any narrative that the processes are unrelated.
records.policy_implication: Suggests that a resolution to the refugee and displacement issue is intrinsically linked to addressing the settlement policy.

records.record_text: The Commission is convinced that in the implementation of its policy of settlements, Israel has resorted to methods - often coercive and sometimes more subtle - which included the control of water resources, the seizure of private properties, the destruction of houses and the banishment of persons, and has shown disregard for basic human rights, including in particular the right of the refugees to return to their homeland.
records.actor_source: Security Council Commission established under resolution 446 (1979)
records.policy_implication: These findings could form the basis for investigations by human rights bodies and provide evidence for legal challenges.

records.record_text: The land seized by the Israeli authorities as a whole, either specifically for the establishment of those settlements or for other stated reasons, covers 27 per cent of the occupied West Bank and the quasi-totality of the Golan Heights.
records.actor_source: Security Council Commission established under resolution 446 (1979)
records.policy_implication: The quantification of land seizure demonstrates the large scale of the settlement enterprise and its physical impact on the territory.

records.record_text: In consideration Of the circumstances in which resolution 446 (1979) had been adopted, the Government of Israel had rejected that resolution in its entirety and accordingly could not extend any form of co-operation to a Commission set up under it.
records.actor_target: Security Council Commission established under resolution 446 (1979)
records.political_signal: Israel's non-cooperation is a clear signal of its rejection of the Security Council's authority and consensus on this issue.
records.policy_implication: This action significantly hampered the Commission's ability to conduct its investigation, particularly its inability to visit the occupied territories.

records.record_text: On the basis of the information received, the Commission is convinced that a number of settlements were established on privately-owned land and not only on public land.
records.actor_source: Security Council Commission established under resolution 446 (1979)
records.policy_implication: This finding directly contradicts potential Israeli claims of only using state or public land, highlighting the seizure of private property as a key component of the settlement policy.

records.record_text: The settlement policy has brought drastic and adverse changes to the economic and social pattern of the daily life of the remaining Arab population. As a mere example of that evolution, the Commission was informed that a number of Arab landowners were now compelled to earn their living and that of their family by working on their own land as the hired employees of the Israeli settlers.
records.actor_source: Security Council Commission established under resolution 446 (1979)
records.policy_implication: Highlights the transformation of the local economy from subsistence and ownership to wage labor, indicating a loss of economic independence and social status for the Palestinian population.

records.record_text: The Commission also perceived a deep sense of despair and helplessness, primarily among Palestinian refugees. This stems from the realization that Israel's policy with regard to the occupied Arab territories and more particularly its policy of continuing to establish more settlements is unabated and undaunted either by United Nations decisions or any other external factor.
records.actor_source: Security Council Commission established under resolution 446 (1979)
records.political_signal: The report highlights the psychological impact of the settlement policy and the perceived impunity of Israel, which erodes faith in international solutions and could fuel extremism.
records.policy_implication: Warns that failure to address the issue effectively could have significant consequences for regional stability.

records.record_text: The Egyptian Government had informed the United States and Israel that it condemned the settlement policy and insisted that those settlements should be removed. This had been achieved in the case of the settlements established in Sinai, and for its part, Egypt would endeavour to have them removed from all the Arab territories, including Arab Jerusalem.
records.actor_source: Government of the Arab Republic of Egypt
records.political_signal: Egypt positions its bilateral achievement on Sinai settlements as a precedent to be applied to all occupied territories, framing its separate peace as part of a comprehensive solution.

records.record_text: The policy of Israel in that regard was to consider the area as one geological basin. Accordingly, it had adopted certain restrictive policies against the Arab farmers, such as the interdiction of drilling artesian wells without a special permit. By contrast Israeli authorities had drilled 24 wells for the exclusive use of Jewish settlers, mostly in the Jordan Valley, thus reducing considerably the amount of water available to Arab farmers.
records.actor_source: Adrian Abu Odeh, Minister of Information of Jordan
records.policy_implication: The issue of water control is identified as a critical tool of coercion and economic pressure, with significant implications for the viability of Palestinian agriculture and communities.

records.record_text: Through the establishment of three successive belts of settlements, Israel was creating protective pockets between Jerusalem and the Jordan River. As a result of this, it was 'compartmenting' the Arab population.
records.policy_implication: This describes a strategic objective of the settlement policy: the fragmentation of Palestinian territorial contiguity, which directly undermines the basis for a viable future state.

mission_title: Report of the Mission to Botswana

mission_analytics.mission_subtype: Needs Assessment
main_risks: Deteriorating security on the border with Southern Rhodesia, including armed incursions, jeopardizing the lives and property of Botswana nationals.
Forced diversion of 70% of domestic development funds to unplanned security needs, threatening the country's normal development plan.
Potential collapse of Botswana's economy due to its dependency on the Rhodesia-operated railway, which is at risk of disruption or discontinuance.
Threat to Botswana's vital beef industry from foot-and-mouth disease spreading from Southern Rhodesia due to a decline in veterinary controls there.
Severe strain on national resources and infrastructure from a large and increasing influx of refugees from Southern Rhodesia and South Africa.
Impending food shortages due to drought and the risk of disruption to food imports.
main_commitments: The mission recommended a comprehensive package of emergency projects for international funding, totaling approximately $25.6 million in capital costs.
A call for international donors to provide general programme assistance or project-based funding to cover the development budget shortfall caused by the diversion of funds to security.
The Government of Botswana decided to substantially expand its Police Mobile Unit to counter security threats from Southern Rhodesia.
The mission chief engaged with the EEC, the UK, and the Commonwealth to discuss programmes of assistance to Botswana.
main_policy_signals: The report validates Botswana's complaint to the Security Council regarding violations of its territorial sovereignty by the illegal regime in Southern Rhodesia.
It frames international assistance to Botswana not just as development aid, but as a direct response to the security and economic consequences of the Southern Rhodesia crisis.
The mission signals strong UN solidarity with a frontline state facing economic hardship due to its geopolitical position and adherence to international law.
It underscores the interconnectedness of security, economic development, and humanitarian stability in the Southern Africa region.
mission_analytics.summary_assessment: Mandated by Security Council resolution 403 (1977), the mission conducted a 14-day needs assessment in Botswana to evaluate the economic hardship resulting from security threats posed by the illegal regime in Southern Rhodesia. Through extensive field visits and high-level consultations, the mission verified Botswana's claims of border violations and quantified the severe economic impact, noting that 70% of domestic development funds were being diverted to unplanned security expenditures. The report identifies critical risks to Botswana's economy, including the potential disruption of the railway and the threat of disease to its vital beef industry, alongside a growing refugee crisis. The mission's primary outcome is a detailed recommendation for approximately $53 million in international assistance, comprising both funding for emergency projects (railway, food security, veterinary control, refugee facilities) and programme support to enable Botswana's normal development to continue. The report effectively translates a security complaint into a comprehensive economic and humanitarian assistance plan for the international community.

activities.activity_description: The Mission's programme in Botswana began with a full briefing by the President- of the Republic of Botswana.
Daily meetings were held with ministers and officials concerned with the work of the Mission.
In the course of its stay, the Mission visited Francistown.
At Francistown the Mission inspected the refugee reception centre and had discussions with government officials.

The rlission also drove some 50 kilometres along the border in the area where many of the incidents had occurred and where some of the projects, which have been made necessary by the deteriorating security situation, will be located.
The Mission was able to visit a number of villajies near the border with Southern Rhodesia...
...and to in-herview a number of villagers, farmers and traders who had been affected by acts of provocation and harassment by the forces of the illegal r&&x in Southern Rhodesia.
Before departinK from Gaborone, the Chief of Mission met with heads of diplomatic missions in Botswana to provide them with information on the Xission and its work.

On kis way to New York, the Chief of Mission had meetings to discuss programmes of assistance to Botswana with Commissioner C. Cheysson of the European Economic Community (EEC), with the Rt. Hon. Judith Hart, Minister of Overseas Development of the United Kingdom, and with Mr. S. S. Ramphal, Commonwealth Secretary-General.

actors_met.actor_name: President of the Republic of Botswana, Sir Seretse Khama
Ministers and officials of the Government of Botswana
Villagers, farmers and traders in border areas

records.record_text: The Foreirn Minister of Eotswana detailed some 36 violations of Botswana's territorial integrity in recent years. He stated that when these incidents first began they were directed at refugees from Southern Rhodesia, but that they are now directed also at Botswana nationals. He reported that incidents have increased in frequency and seriousness in recent months.
records.policy_implication: Provides the initial justification for the Security Council's engagement and the mission's mandate.

records.record_text: The Government of Botswana had decided to increase substantially the size of its police mobile unit to enable Botswalia to put up greater resistance to the activities of the forces of the illegal regime in Southern Rhodesia.
records.political_signal: Signals Botswana's intent to defend its territory while highlighting the unplanned nature of this expenditure.
records.policy_implication: This decision forms the basis for the 'diversion of funds' argument central to the mission's mandate.

records.record_text: The expansion of the police mobile unit would cost approximately P 25 million (some $29 million) in a four-year period which would substantially reduce the resources available for their development programme.
records.policy_implication: Establishes the core problem of economic hardship that the mission was tasked to assess.

records.record_text: The security situation in the areas bordering with Southern Rhodesia has deteriorated sharply in the past year.
records.policy_implication: Mission's core finding, validating Botswana's complaint and providing the basis for its recommendations.

records.record_text: The unplanned a& unbudgeted costs to the Government of Botswana of expanding the Police Mobile Unit... will amount to some $16.3 million on capital account and $3.4 million annually on current account.
records.policy_implication: Quantifies the financial diversion, providing a concrete basis for calculating assistance needs.

records.record_text: When the Mission visited the transit centre on 18 February 1977, there were 7119 persons accommodated there... The Mission found living conditions to be hopelessly inadequate, with sanitation and hygiene facilities totally unsatisfactory. The centre was overcrowded...
records.policy_implication: Provides direct evidence for the urgent need for recommended refugee assistance projects.

records.record_text: The Mission estimEttes that some $27.98 million will need to be diverted to unplanned and unbudgeted security needs, to provide protection, transport and supervision for refugees, arid to meet part of the recurrent costs Of emerp;ency projects during the first three years of the 1976-1981 plan period. This will amount to 70 per cent of the domestic resources which it was planned to use for normal development.
records.policy_implication: This is the central analytical finding, quantifying the scale of the economic hardship and directly linking it to the need for international assistance to cover the development gap.

records.record_text: The economy of Bo-Lswana is very open and heavily dependent on imports and exports. This means that the continued operation of the railway through Botswana now operated by Rhodesia Railways is extremely important as there would be a grave risk to the economy if the services were interrupted or discontinued.
records.policy_implication: Identifies a critical economic vulnerability directly linked to the regional conflict, justifying a major component of the recommended emergency assistance.

records.record_text: It will therefore be necessary to develop a capability to operate the railway in an emergency. This will cost some $16.3 million, as well as stand-by credits for meeting operating losses...
records.policy_implication: Proposes a specific, high-cost project to mitigate a key strategic risk, forming a cornerstone of the assistance package.

records.record_text: The risk of an F?Q [foot-and-mouth disease] outbreag crossing the border into Cotswana is very high... The effect of a foot-and-.mouth disease outbreak... would be disastrous for the livestock industry in Botswana.
records.policy_implication: Highlights an indirect but potentially catastrophic economic consequence of the deteriorating situation in Southern Rhodesia, justifying a package of veterinary control projects.

records.record_text: The Mission believes that there are four major ways in which the international community could assist Bctswana to carry out its normal development projects in the new circumstances: (a) General programme assistance... (is) Project assistance for projects included in the National Development Plan... (c) Assistance in carrying out the emergency projects; (d) Financing agencies agreeing to reduce cm waive local cost contributions...
records.political_signal: Provides a clear, actionable roadmap for donors to follow in responding to the report's findings.
records.policy_implication: Offers flexible options for donors, increasing the likelihood of a positive response by accommodating different aid modalities.

records.record_text: All the projects in the core programme which the Government of Botswana intended to finance from the Domestic Development Fund and the total costs of projects in the core programme for which funding was still to be arranged, as well as the emergency projects recommended in this report, will need to be financed by external sources if Botswana is to be enabled to carry out its normal development as envisaged in Security Council resolution 403 (1977).
records.policy_implication: This is the ultimate policy conclusion of the report, explicitly defining the scope of international assistance required to fulfill the mandate of SCR 403 (1977).

records.record_text: The Government of Botswana is therefore requesting 7,000 tons of sorghum and maize, for delivery from August onwards for selective famine relief for those sections of the population who have experienced crop failure and cannot afford to buy imported grains.
records.policy_implication: The mission endorses this request by including it as a recommended emergency project (Project 8).

records.record_text: The Mission was able to visit a number of villajies near the border with Southern Rhodesia, and to in-herview a number of villagers, farmers and traders who had been affected by acts of provocation and harassment... They considered it dangerous to water their livestock and cultivate their crops. Indeed, many homes were abandoned...
records.policy_implication: Provides a human-level account of the impact of border insecurity, strengthening the justification for security and development projects in the area.

mission_title: Report of the Security Council Special Mission to the People's Republic of Benin established under resolution 404 (1977)

mission_analytics.mission_subtype: Fact-finding on an armed incident
main_risks: The use of mercenaries to destabilize sovereign states, particularly small countries.
The potential for similar mercenary operations to be conducted elsewhere.
Unverified but serious allegations of complicity by officials in third countries in staging the attack.
main_commitments: The Security Council decided to remain seized of the question.
The Government of Benin requested that the UN assume responsibility for compensation for damages and take measures to prevent the recurrence of such acts.
The Government of Benin committed to transmitting a full evaluation of damages to the Special Mission at a later date.
main_policy_signals: The establishment of the Special Mission itself signaled the Security Council's serious concern over the attack.
The Council's affirmation that Benin's territorial integrity and political independence must be respected.
Broad condemnation of the attack by the Non-Aligned Movement, the Arab Group, and the African Group, framing it as aggression against all African and third-world states.
mission_analytics.summary_assessment: The Special Mission conducted an extensive on-the-ground investigation in Cotonou to investigate the armed attack of 16 January 1977. Through site visits, examination of physical evidence, and extensive testimony, the mission conclusively determined that Benin was the victim of aggression by an external mercenary force whose primary objective was to overthrow the government. The mission collected substantial evidence, including detailed testimony from a captured mercenary and abandoned documents, which pointed to a complex international operation involving recruitment in Europe and Africa, training at a base near Marrakesh, Morocco, and staging through Gabon. While presenting this highly suggestive evidence, the mission noted its mandate did not permit full verification, thereby handing the politically sensitive findings to the Security Council for further consideration.

activities.activity_description: On 11 February 1977, the Special Mission held a meeting at Headquarters to discuss the issues arising from its mandate and to make necessary arrangements for its journey to Benin.
On 17 February, H.E. Mr. Mathieu Kérékou, President and head of State and Government of the People's Republic of Benin received the members of the Special Mission.

On 17 February, the members of the Special Mission held a meeting with the Committee Established by the Government of Benin for the Special Mission of the Security Council to discuss the Mission's programme of work.

On 17 February, the Mission paid a visit to the dean of the diplomatic corps, the Ambassador of France to the People's Republic of Benin, to arrange the hearing of statements by heads of diplomatic missions.
On 18 February, the Special Mission spent the whole day hearing the testimony from witnesses to the events of 16 January.
On 19 and 24 February, the Special Mission heard the testimony of a person presented as having been a member of the attacking force, taken prisoner on 16 January.
On 19 and 24 February, the members of the Special Mission inspected armaments, munitions and supplies which were presented as having been left behind by the attacking force.

On 20 and 21 February, the Special Mission devoted the whole day to visiting sites of military action on 16 January, hearing explanations from the competent authorities, talking with witnesses and persons wounded along the route of the attackers.
On 20 February, the Special Mission visited a morgue where there were corpses of two members of the attacking force killed on 16 January.
On 21 and 23 February, the Special Mission heard statements by several heads of diplomatic missions at Cotonou.
On 21 and 22 February, the Special Mission examined documentation presented to them as having been left behind in Cotonou by the attacking force on 16 January.
On 23 February, the Mission inspected damage done on 16 January by weapons fire to the residence of the Ambassador of the United States at Cotonou.
On 21, 24 February, the members of the Special Mission held working sessions with the Benin Committee for the Special Mission.
